title: From a settled specification to reviewed code
lead: Use this when the questions are answered and what is left is work. Each ticket here is a slice of work that ends in running code with its own check. A ticket that still asks a question is a different kind of ticket and belongs to the wayfinder guide; if one turns up halfway, stop building and go there.
scenario: A small app called Trail Report lets hikers post and read recent trail conditions. Its specification is settled. The app, the spec and every result below are invented.
input: The Trail Report spec is settled. Break it into tickets and get it built.

steps.label: Cut the spec into thin slices
steps.text: Each slice goes through every layer a little: a form, a store and a page, not all the stores first and all the pages last. Each states what blocks it and how you would check it alone. The draft has five slices: post a report, list a trail's reports, flag a wrong report, hide reports older than 14 days, and a weekly digest.

steps.label: Approve the breakdown
steps.text: Nothing is published until you approve the granularity and the blocking edges. In the draft, flagging waited for the list slice. You point out that a flag only needs a stored report, so it now waits for the first slice alone. That one edge is what lets two slices run side by side. You also decline a sixth slice, photo attachments, and leave it out of scope.

steps.label: Choose how to build
steps.text: There are two ways to build, and they are different choices. One slice at a time keeps you in each session and suits a chain of dependent slices or a spec you do not yet trust. The whole graph at once suits a settled spec with slices that can run together. Here, after the first slice, two slices are free to run together, and you trust the spec. Both ways are shown next so you can see what each does.

steps.label: Choice A: one ticket in one session
steps.text: The session reads the slice, says its title back, and builds only that. It writes the check first, makes it pass, runs the whole test suite once at the end, then reviews the result. For slice 1 it commits to your current branch. For slice 2 you start another session. Nothing runs in parallel, and you see every slice finish.

steps.label: Choice B: the whole graph on one branch
steps.text: A fresh agent takes each slice in its own working copy, and a merger folds finished slices onto one integration branch. Slice 1 goes first because nothing else is free. When it merges, slices 2 and 4 start together. Slice 3 waits for 2, and slice 5 waits for both 2 and 3. A review pass and one fixer run at the end, and the result is a draft change marked ready for review. It stops there; merging is yours.

steps.label: Inside every slice, check first
steps.text: Whichever way you chose, each slice builds the same way. Slice 1 starts with a test that posts a report for a trail and reads it back, and it fails because nothing stores reports yet. The smallest code that passes is written, then the next behavior. The test sits at the store's public interface, so it survives a rewrite of what is behind it.

steps.label: Review on two separate axes
steps.text: Two reviewers look at everything since the integration branch left the main line, and their reports stay apart. Standards asks whether the code follows the repository's own written conventions. Spec asks whether it does what the specification says. A change can pass one and fail the other, so a single blended score would hide the problem.

steps.label: Read both reports and decide
steps.text: You read the two lists. You decide what gets fixed now, what is recorded for later and what is wrong with the review itself. Merging the branch is also your call, after this reading.

steps.label: The reviewed branch
steps.text: One integration branch with five slices on it, each with a passing check, and a two-part review that someone else can read. It is a candidate for merge, not a merged change.

steps.label: Photos and spam flags
steps.text: Photo attachments are out of scope. Nobody has decided what happens when someone flags every report on a trail. If the second one blocks a slice, it is a decision, not work, and it goes to a decision map.

settled: Five slices, and the edges between them.
Flagging needs a stored report, not the list page.
open: What to do about one person flagging every report on a trail.

build.title: The slices and what blocks them
build.lead: Every slice is work with its own check. Read the edges as 'cannot start until'. A slice with no blocker can start now.

plates.caption: Five invented slices. An arrow means the slice at its tail must finish before the slice at its head can start.

slices.title: Post a report
slices.verify: a test posts a report for one trail and reads it back.

slices.title: List a trail's reports
slices.verify: a test seeds three reports and checks the page lists them newest first.

slices.title: Flag a wrong report
slices.verify: a test flags a stored report twice and checks that it no longer shows.

slices.title: Hide old reports
slices.verify: a test with a fixed clock checks that a 15-day-old report is hidden and a 13-day-old one is shown.

slices.title: Weekly digest
slices.verify: a test compares the digest built from fixed sample reports with the expected text.

build.parallel: Only slice 1 can start now. When it is done, slices 2 and 4 can run side by side. Slice 3 waits for 2, and slice 5 waits for 2 and 3. Slice 4 never blocks the others, so it can finish at any time. Running slices in parallel only helps where the edges allow it; the edges are the plan.

artifact.title: Review summary (invented example)
lines: Branch: trail-report-build, five slices merged onto it, all five checks passing.
Standards: one finding. Date arithmetic is written out in two files; the repository's conventions ask for the shared date helper.
Spec: one finding. The spec says reports older than 14 days are hidden. The code hides a report on day 14 itself, one day early.
Counts: Standards 1, Spec 1. Neither report was folded into the other.
Status: ready for a person to read. Not merged.

stop: You are done when every slice's own check passes on the integration branch, both review reports exist and each finding is fixed or written down, and you have read them. Merging is not part of this. If a slice cannot be checked on its own, send it back to be re-cut, because it is hiding a question.
limits: The app and every result are invented. I did not run this against production code, and nothing here shows how long a real build takes. Slices come from a spec, so a wrong spec produces five tidy slices of the wrong thing. Parallel agents cost more than one and cannot fix a bad edge. tdd and code-review are my customized copies; the registry notes how each differs from the published one. Decision tickets, where the work is a question, are a different graph: see the wayfinder guide.
